synthesis.headline: Pattern re-amplifies into a fall block: a southern-Rockies cutoff and departing Great Lakes low sandwich an eastern ridge, with the heat ridge set to contract toward the Southwest
synthesis.narrative:
The big picture today is a pattern that has re-blocked after yesterday's brief flattening. At 500 mb a genuine cutoff low sits over the central and southern Rockies, closed off near 530 dam over Colorado-New Mexico and slightly negatively tilted, flanked by a Pacific-coast ridge to its west and a broad eastern ridge (588 dam and higher over the Great Lakes and Mid-Atlantic) to its east. Those flanking ridges are retarding eastward progress and give the flow a blocked rather than progressive character, but the western ridge and eastern cutoff are not stacked at the same longitude, so this is not a Rex block — just a strongly amplified, high-over-low arrangement. Running out ahead of the western cutoff is the northern-stream upper low now over the upper Great Lakes and northern Plains, which the Air Mass RGB catches as a tight cyclonic swirl of cold tops with a compact dry streamer curling around its western and southern flank. That departing low is today's principal weather-maker.

The centers of action are three. First, the northern-tier system anchors a slow front and repeated convection producing the day's heaviest-rain and flash-flood threat from the northern/central Rockies and Plains through the Midwest, Ohio Valley and Mid-Atlantic, made worse by already-saturated soils. Second, severe weather is a Slight-risk story: the southern-Rockies trough moving into the central High Plains supports afternoon supercells with 1-2.5 inch hail from eastern Colorado into western Kansas, while moderate buoyancy and shear along the front bring severe wind gusts and hail across Oklahoma, the Ozarks and into the Ohio Valley. Third, an offshore/coastal cutoff near the Southeast Atlantic seaboard is firing deep convection over coastal Georgia and the adjacent western Atlantic; NHC is not flagging it for tropical development, and it lines up with CPC's isolated cool lean over the Carolinas and Virginia. In Canada the story is equally active: a vigorous 976 hPa Pacific low is driving a cold front toward the BC coast and Pacific Northwest, an important incoming maker for the West; a Hudson Bay low trails fronts into Manitoba and Ontario; and a stratospheric-intrusion-wrapped extratropical cyclone northeast of the Maritimes keeps a tight Atlantic-Canada gradient.

Upstairs, the jet corridor implied by the tight height gradient runs along the northern periphery of the central cutoff and curves northeast across the northern tier at roughly 60-80 knots — that is the forcing rail carrying the northern rain shield eastward. The broad orange-red drying across the western and central CONUS on the Air Mass RGB is warm-season, anticyclonic ridge-top dry air given its extent, not a stratospheric intrusion; the only compact, cyclonically curved dry feature over the lower 48 is the one wrapping the Great Lakes low, and the one genuine stratospheric intrusion on the full disk is well downstream on the Maritimes cyclone. On evolution, read the two ensemble leads against each other: the 6-10 day (Sep 25-29) rebuilds a broad western ridge covering North America to about the 100th meridian with its positive-anomaly core over the Southwest and northwestern Mexico, while the 8-14 day (Sep 27-Oct 3) shrinks that ridge back to the Southwest and northern Mexico, leaving western Canada and the northern Plains near-neutral to weakly negative beneath a deep, amplified Arctic low. That pair says the same thing yesterday's did: the heat ridge is genuinely contracting and retreating southwestward rather than rebuilding in the north, and the WPC extended discussion frames the coming week as an amplified, blocky autumn regime with wet Northwest and Eastern troughs sandwiching a southern-tier ridge.
synthesis.climate_context: ENSO has settled into a strong El Niño, with the ONI reaching roughly +1.8 by summer 2026 after swinging out of last winter's weak La Niña. The tropics fit that state cleanly just past the climatological peak of hurricane season: the Atlantic is quiet apart from Tropical Storm Fay near the Azores, with no development expected over the next seven days, while the East Pacific stays busy — Tropical Storm Odalys southwest of Baja, a broad low south of Manzanillo likely to become a depression within 24 hours, and reviving remnants of TD 15-E east of Hawaii at 60 percent over seven days — the textbook El Niño basin split. Seasonally, the North American Monsoon is reloading where the southern-Rockies cutoff overlaps surging Pacific and Gulf moisture, the driver behind next week's New Mexico flooding threat, and late-season severe weather continues in its expected northern-tier, ridge-periphery and frontal mode rather than as deep-Plains outbreaks. Teleconnections remain a weak warm-season cross-check: a notably negative NAO (7-day mean near -1.01) is consistent with the eastern cutoff persisting rather than escaping downstream, a weakly negative PNA offers modest support for the eastern trough, and a near-neutral AO carries little weight — none of these are the basis for the story the height and PV fields already tell.
synthesis.regional_notes: SPC has no active mesoscale discussions and none in the past six hours; today's severe risk is Slight only, focused on High Plains supercells (1-2.5 inch hail) from eastern Colorado into western Kansas, wind and hail across Oklahoma and the Ozarks, and isolated wind into the Ohio Valley. Flash flooding over saturated soils is the larger sub-synoptic concern along the northern-tier-to-Mid-Atlantic rain axis, with the wet regime continuing over south Florida and the Keys. Heat and humidity linger across the central and southern Plains and Tennessee Valley. Looking a few days out, WPC advertises a monsoon flooding threat for New Mexico and the southern Rockies/High Plains as Pacific and Gulf moisture combine (Marginal-to-Slight excessive-rainfall risk Wednesday-Thursday), plus a Mid-Atlantic/Northeast coastal low with a strong Quebec high driving a cold-air-damming wedge, highs in the 50s-60s, and coastal-flood potential midweek. In Canada, watch the incoming BC/Pacific Northwest frontal system and the Manitoba-Ontario convergence zone off the Hudson Bay low.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This 0900Z 20 September 2026 WPC surface analysis shows a sprawling 1029 mb high dominating the northern Plains and upper Midwest, with a secondary 1022 mb high over the Canadian Rockies and a robust 1025 mb high anchored off the New England coast — together producing a notably strong pressure gradient and implied northwesterly flow across much of the central and eastern US. The tightest gradient on the chart is along the Atlantic seaboard where the offshore high and an inland low near the Tennessee-Kentucky border (around 1010-1012 mb) are in close proximity, indicated by the compressed isobars there and consistent with enhanced low-level convergence and lift along what appears to be a stalled or slow-moving front in that corridor. A surface low near the southern Rockies-New Mexico area, reading near 1008 mb, anchors a cold front extending southward into Texas and a warm front or stationary boundary pushing eastward across the Gulf states, and the warm, moist air mass across the Gulf Coast and lower Mississippi Valley — dewpoints implied by the plotted temperatures reaching the mid-70s F — is being underrun by that frontal boundary, focusing the primary moisture and lift threat across the Southeast and Gulf Coast region. Across the interior West, the 1007 mb low off the California coast and a separate 1011 mb low over the Great Basin define a broad trough with slack gradients through the Desert Southwest, suggesting limited organized lift there despite the thermal low pressure. The northern tier from the Rockies eastward sits under the influence of the strong 1029 mb anticyclone with widely spaced isobars and unseasonably cool temperatures, consistent with surface subsidence and suppressed convection across that zone.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This CMC surface analysis valid 0000Z 20 September 2026 shows a vigorous low centered near 976 hPa in the north-central Pacific, well west of the British Columbia coast, with a tightly wound isobar field and an associated frontal system that trails southeastward; the cold front appears to be pushing toward the BC coast and the Pacific Northwest, suggesting an active incoming weather maker for western Canada within the next day or so. Over what appears to be the western Canadian interior and the northern Prairie provinces, a high near 1026-1027 hPa is positioned, with relatively relaxed gradients suggesting settled conditions there at analysis time. Across the upper portion of the chart — consistent with the Arctic Ocean and Canadian Archipelago given the polar projection — several lows in the 980-998 hPa range are present, but their placement far poleward means they are not directly forcing provincial weather. A secondary low cluster near 997-998 hPa sits in a position that, judging from the surrounding coastline geometry, appears to lie over or just west of Hudson Bay, with frontal boundaries trailing southward into the central United States and implying a zone of lift and moisture convergence across Manitoba and Ontario. Along the Atlantic margin, the isobars tighten noticeably between a high near 1027 hPa to the north and the broader low pressure field to the south, pointing to an elevated pressure gradient across Atlantic Canada.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary: At 1200 UTC 20 September 2026, the 500 mb pattern shows a broad longwave trough centered roughly over the central and southern Rockies, with heights falling to near 530 dam over the Colorado-New Mexico area and closed contours visible, indicating a genuine cutoff low isolated from the main westerly flow rather than an open shortwave. The contour geometry around this feature shows a slightly negative tilt, with the axis oriented from northwest to southeast. A broad ridge dominates the eastern third of the country, with heights reaching 588 dam or higher across the Great Lakes and Mid-Atlantic region, and a second ridge axis is apparent over the Pacific coast; together these flanking ridges are retarding eastward progression of the central trough, giving the overall pattern a blocked rather than progressive character, though the western ridge and eastern cutoff are not meridionally stacked at the same longitude and so do not constitute a classical Rex block. A low pressure center marked near the southeast Atlantic seaboard, with surrounding heights near 587 dam, appears largely cutoff from the main flow and is consistent with a tropical or subtropical cyclone given its position; temperatures plotted near it are relatively warm compared to the continental interior. No discrete jet streak axes are explicitly plotted, but the implied jet corridor, inferred from the tight height gradient, runs along the northern periphery of the central cutoff and curves northeastward across the northern tier states, with wind observations near that zone suggesting speeds on the order of 60-80 knots.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 AirMass RGB from 20 Sep 2026 at 13:21Z shows a broad orange-red dry airmass signature dominating the western and central CONUS, consistent with a deep, dry upper ridge covering the Desert Southwest through the southern Plains, but this coloring reflects warm, dry mid-to-upper tropospheric air under the ridge rather than a stratospheric intrusion. The sharpest and most compelling dry feature is a compact, curved orange-red streamer wrapping cyclonically around what appears to be a closed low or trough center positioned near the upper Great Lakes region, where a swirl of higher cold cloud tops in white-green is visible; the leading edge of this dry intrusion on the western and southern flank of that system marks the likely jet corridor. A well-defined cyclonic cloud swirl with cold white tops is visible over the Great Lakes area, and a separate area of deep convective towers with bright white tops is located over coastal Georgia and the adjacent western Atlantic, consistent with an organized convective system or tropical feature. Additional clusters of deep convection with cold white tops are visible over the northwestern Caribbean and Hispaniola in the lower right of the image. The green moisture signal is continuous from the Gulf of Mexico northward into the eastern CONUS east of the central dry region, feeding both the Great Lakes system and the coastal convection.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 AirMass RGB from 20 September 2026 at 1310Z shows a pronounced airmass contrast across the North Atlantic, where a vigorous extratropical cyclone northeast of the Canadian Maritimes displays the classic comma-head structure with bright white high cloud wrapping into a well-defined dry-air slot rendered in deep orange-red on its western flank — the compact, cyclonically curved geometry there is consistent with a stratospheric intrusion along the trough axis. Across Canada, a broad blue-to-orange gradient marks the polar front, with cold dry upper-tropospheric air (dark blue) dominating the high Arctic and a sharper boundary visible over the Hudson Bay region where the flow appears to curve cyclonically around a trough. In the tropics, scattered clusters of white convective tops are visible over southern Mexico, Central America, and the northern Amazon basin, embedded in the broad green moisture field, with no single organized tropical wave or circulation standing out clearly at this scale in the eastern Pacific or Atlantic at this time. The southern hemisphere extratropics show an active westerly belt: a well-developed cyclone with a curved cloud band is visible near the southern tip of South America, and deep red-orange air on the equatorward side of the Southern Ocean storm track is consistent with dry subsiding air within the mid-latitude ridge rather than a stratospheric intrusion given its broad, diffuse extent.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary: The dominant feature is a broad above-normal temperature signal covering most of the contiguous United States from the Rockies eastward through the central Plains and into the upper Midwest, with the highest probabilities — 80 to 90 percent — concentrated over Texas, Oklahoma, Louisiana, and adjacent Gulf Coast states, and a secondary 80-90 percent core extending through the northern Plains and upper Great Lakes region. The western interior from roughly the Great Basin through the central Rockies also carries 60-70 percent above-normal odds, while the Pacific Northwest and northern California show only leaning-above signals at 33-40 percent, and coastal Washington and Oregon verge on near normal. The lone below-normal signal sits over the Carolinas and Virginia at 33-40 percent probability, a relatively weak leaning that stands out as an isolated cool exception on the Southeast Atlantic seaboard. The spatial coherence and intensity of the above-normal probabilities across such a wide interior domain — particularly the dual high-confidence cores over the southern Plains and upper Midwest — are consistent with a persistent amplified upper-level ridge, implying the CPC guidance does not favor a meaningful pattern breakdown through September 25-29. Alaska's southcentral region carries a 40-50 percent above-normal signal, and Hawaii shows 70-80 percent above normal, while the Aleutians show a leaning-above signal.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary: This 6-10 day (25-29 September 2026) 500 mb height and anomaly forecast shows a deep, closed cyclone centered over the central Canadian Arctic, with the innermost contour near 516 dam and surrounding contours tightly packed, indicating a pronounced negative height anomaly center there; the blue dashed anomaly contours confirm negative departures reaching at least -90 dam in the chart's units, but given that anomalies run to single or low double digits in dam, those blue dashed labels (reading -90, -120) are almost certainly plotted in meters, placing the anomaly core near -9 to -12 dam, which is a strong but physically plausible departure. A broad ridge is positioned over the western interior of North America, with the ridge axis running roughly north-south near the Pacific Coast into the U.S. Great Basin, and the 570 dam contour extending well northward into the Canadian Rockies; the positive anomaly center (red dashed contours labeled roughly +50 to +90 in the same meter units, so +5 to +9 dam) sits over the southwestern U.S. and northwestern Mexico, suggesting the western ridge remains amplified and displaced well southward rather than retreating poleward. The zero-anomaly line, visible where the dashed contours transition from positive (red) to negative (blue), crosses the continent roughly along a north-south line near the 100th meridian, meaning positive departures cover the full breadth of western North America from the Pacific coast to the central Plains. The trough axis extends southward from the Arctic low into the eastern two-thirds of Canada and curves toward the Great Lakes region, with a secondary implied trough axis evident along the U.S. East Coast where heights fall to near 532-534 dam. Overall the pattern is highly amplified, not trending toward zonal flow: the large meridional height gradient between the western ridge and the eastern trough, combined with the strongly negative Arctic center, describes an amplified, split-flow regime rather than a flat westerly pattern.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary: This chart is a 500 mb heights and anomalies prognostic valid 27 Sep – 03 Oct 2026, made 19 Sep 2026, showing ensemble-mean geopotential heights in dam (green contours, 60 dam intervals) and height anomalies in dam (dashed contours, presumably also labeled). The dominant feature is a deep closed low centered over the central Canadian Arctic, with heights near 522 dam at its core; surrounding it, height contours amplify strongly downstream, producing a sharp trough axis oriented roughly north-south through central Canada and a well-developed ridge to its east across the North Atlantic. Over the western third of North America, height contours are steeply tilted and broadly spaced, indicating the ridge axis has retreated well to the southwest — the implied ridge core sits over the U.S. Southwest and northern Mexico near the 588 dam contour, not over the northern Rockies or northern Plains, which fall on the eastern flank of this western ridge and poleward approach of the trough. Reading the dashed anomaly contours, a significant negative anomaly center of roughly −9 to −10 dam (the innermost closed dashed contour reads near −90 on the chart's scale, which given the stated dam interval and CPC convention I interpret as −9 dam) appears co-located with the Arctic low, while positive anomalies of similar magnitude appear to the east over the North Atlantic; western Canada through the northern Plains shows near-neutral to weakly negative anomaly, confirming the absence of a positive height anomaly ridge centered over that region in this forecast period.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: Upper-level low and shortwave trough moving eastward across northern Plains through Sunday. Slow-moving frontal boundary and repeated convection will produce excessive rainfall and flash flooding threat across northern/central Rockies, Plains, Midwest, Ohio Valley, and Mid-Atlantic through Sunday, especially over saturated soils. Severe thunderstorm threat including hail and severe winds across central/southern Plains into Ohio Valley and Mid-Atlantic. Monday: frontal system pushes southeast with organized convection continuing; excessive rainfall concerns shift toward Mid-Atlantic and southern Plains, while severe thunderstorm threat moves into central/southern Appalachians and Southeast. Heat and humidity persist across central/southern Plains and Tennessee Valley.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary: Slight risk of severe thunderstorms across Oklahoma and eastern Colorado into far western Kansas, with isolated severe threat in southern Plains and Ozarks extending into Ohio Valley. Wind gusts and large hail are primary hazards. In Oklahoma, moderate buoyancy and sufficient shear support severe wind gusts this afternoon into evening, with strongest gusts expected in southern OK. Central High Plains: mid-level trough moves in with scattered storms likely by mid-afternoon; supercells probable with primary threat being 1-2.5 inch hail and isolated severe gusts. Ozarks and Ohio Valley: low-amplitude perturbations moving east with a southward-moving cold front; moderate buoyancy expected to develop, mainly isolated wind threat, though some model uncertainty exists regarding low-level flow strengthening.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No organized convective threat is currently being monitored by SPC. No mesoscale discussions have been issued in the past 6 hours.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
ATLANTIC: Tropical Storm Fay, recently upgraded, located several hundred miles southwest of the Azores. No tropical cyclone formation expected over the next 7 days.

EAST PACIFIC: Tropical Storm Odalys newly formed, over 1,000 miles southwest of southern Baja California. A broad low pressure area 400 miles south of Manzanillo shows organized showers and thunderstorms with conducive conditions; tropical depression likely within 24 hours as system moves northward. Remnants of former TD 15-E east-southeast of Hawaiian Islands show limited activity; could develop midweek as conditions improve, with 60 percent formation chance over 7 days.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: ONI values show a transition from weak La Niña conditions (anomaly -0.60°C in NDJ 2025) toward El Niño. Anomalies warm steadily through early 2026, crossing into positive territory by February-March and strengthening significantly. By summer 2026 (JJA), the anomaly reaches +1.80°C, indicating strong El Niño. The warming trend is consistent and pronounced, with the largest jumps occurring April through August 2026.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary: PNA is modestly negative (-0.34), unchanged over the past week, offering weak support for eastern North American trough. AO bounced to +0.53 after dipping negative mid-period, now neutralizing high-latitude blocking tendency. NAO has fallen substantially to -1.01 (7-day mean), down 0.49 from the prior week—notably negative, which could favor eastern cutoff systems persisting rather than escaping downstream. These are summer observations with limited canonical strength, but the NAO's recent descent warrants attention for downstream forecasting implications.
